text:
Trump and several officials visited a detention center in Florida in 2025

After Immigration and Customs Enforcement purchased more than a dozen empty warehouses across the United States, planning to expand capacity to detain people that it deemed to be in the country illegally, it wants to get rid of many of them.

Since President Trump’s administration first sought to increase deportations, it has purchased 11 facilities at a cost of $1 billion — and the New York Times reports that there are plans to offload seven of them.

The seven facilities cost an estimated $700 million, and ICE is hoping to either give them to other federal agencies or sell them. The warehouses in question are located in Michigan and New Jersey.

Former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem championed the initiative, but the Times notes that her successor, Markwayne Mullin, doesn’t share that attitude and has previously said that he doesn’t want to adopt the headline-making tactics of his predecessor.

People detained at the El Paso ICE detention center are reporting inhumane treatment (Image: CBSEveningNews/YouTube)

“From Day 1, D.H.S. has remained singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so,” the Homeland Security Department said in a statement to the Times.

"These heinous criminals, once arrested, should be removed at lightning speed, not housed on American soil at the taxpayer’s expense. D.H.S. is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners."

The Times notes that not only was Noem’s plan expensive, but it conflicted with local communities across the U.S. “Converting industrial space into places that could house thousands of human beings, with water and sewer capacity and proper ventilation” proved to be expensive. The Homeland Security Department’s inspector general is currently investigating the purchases, and the department as a whole is facing a slew of lawsuits citing a lack of oversight and environmental compliance.

“The warehouses were a quick concept to scale up mass deportation,” John Fabbricatore, a former Trump administration official who worked as a senior adviser on immigration issues at the Department of Health and Human Services, said.

“Unfortunately, because of the scale and footprint, the left was able to throw up immediate roadblocks. Immigration detention is necessary for a successful deportation plan, and this was the easiest point for the Democrats to attack and stop that effort.”

Protestors have been vocal about ICE's actions(Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Warehouses in San Antonio and Socorro, Texas; Surprise, Arizona; and Hagerstown, Maryland, are expected to be converted into centers as planned, though a federal judge blocked construction on the Maryland facility for the time being. ICE also has plans to buy immigrant detention facilities from private prison operators that it already contracts with, documents show.

“Clearly the warehouses have caused some serious headaches, with pauses due to state litigation, an I.G. investigation, and no opening date in sight with close to a billion dollars spent,” Claire Trickler-McNulty, a senior ICE official in the Biden administration, said.

“This plan seemed questionable from inception, and the only thing saving it is probably the endless blank check ICE has for detention.”

Tom Homan, White House border czar, told the Times that ICE had hoped that the administration would have 100,000 beds by the end of 2025. However, the agency had detained approximately 70,000 immigrants earlier this year.
